blocks.text: Stochastic gradient descent, SGD, is the foundational optimizer that every more advanced optimizer covered in this module, including AdamW, ultimately builds on, estimating the true gradient using a small random mini-batch rather than the entire dataset at once.

Understanding plain SGD clearly makes the more sophisticated optimizers, Adam, AdamW, Adafactor, and Lion, easier to appreciate as refinements addressing specific limitations of this simple starting point.
1. What Stochastic Gradient Descent Actually Is

blocks.alt: What Stochastic Gradient Descent Actually Is
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100775-237814189.png

SGD estimates the gradient of the loss using a small, randomly selected mini-batch of examples, covered in the earlier Mini-Batches topic, rather than computing the exact gradient over the entire dataset, trading some accuracy in the gradient estimate for dramatically faster, more frequent updates.
2. The Word Stochastic, Where the Randomness Comes From

blocks.alt: The Word Stochastic, Where the Randomness Comes From
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100776-742520887.png

The randomness in stochastic gradient descent comes from using a randomly sampled mini-batch at each step, meaning the gradient estimate at any given step is a noisy approximation of the true gradient over the whole dataset, not an exact calculation.
3. SGD vs Full Batch Gradient Descent

blocks.alt: SGD vs Full Batch Gradient Descent
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100776-848532839.png

Full batch gradient descent computes an exact gradient using the entire dataset before every single update, producing very accurate but very infrequent and computationally expensive updates, while SGD trades that accuracy for far more frequent, cheaper updates using small mini-batches instead.

code.content:
# Plain SGD, the simplest optimizer update rule
weight = weight - learning_rate * gradient_from_minibatch

blocks.text: 4. Why SGD Alone Struggles With Certain Loss Landscapes

blocks.alt: Why SGD Alone Struggles With Certain Loss Landscapes
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100966-350812345.png

Plain SGD can struggle with loss landscapes that have narrow, steep valleys, since it tends to zigzag back and forth across the steep sides rather than moving efficiently along the valley floor toward a good solution, a limitation that motivated the momentum idea covered in the earlier Optimizers topic.
5. SGD With Momentum
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100967-42958681.png

Adding momentum to plain SGD, smoothing updates using a running average of past gradient directions, addresses much of the zigzagging problem, and SGD with momentum remains a genuinely competitive optimizer choice for certain training scenarios even though Adam style optimizers have become more common overall.
6. SGD's Memory Advantage
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100968-902549947.png

Plain SGD needs very little additional memory beyond the gradient itself, no large running estimates the way Adam maintains, covered in detail in the Optimizer States topic later in this module, making it an attractive choice specifically when memory is the tightest constraint.

blocks.text: 7. When SGD Is Still a Reasonable Choice

blocks.alt: When SGD Is Still a Reasonable Choice
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785472100968-56364404.png

SGD, particularly with momentum, remains a reasonable choice specifically when memory is extremely constrained and Adam optimizer state overhead would be too costly, or for certain architectures and tasks where SGD has empirically been shown to generalize as well as or better than adaptive methods.
8. SGD Compared to Adam Style Optimizers

Adam and AdamW, covered in the earlier general Optimizers topic, build directly on the SGD foundation by adding both momentum and an adaptive, per parameter learning rate mechanism, generally converging faster and requiring less manual learning rate tuning than plain SGD, at the cost of the additional memory covered above.
9. SGD in Modern Fine-Tuning Practice

For most fine-tuning projects covered throughout this course, AdamW remains the more commonly reached for default, but understanding SGD clearly is what makes AdamW behavior, and the tradeoffs of the more memory efficient Adafactor and Lion optimizers covered next in this module, genuinely understandable rather than accepted as an unexplained default.
Worked Example

A team working under an extremely tight memory budget, having already applied quantization and LoRA covered in earlier modules, finds that even AdamW modest optimizer state adds up meaningfully across their many trainable parameters.

Switching to plain SGD with momentum for this specific constrained setup frees up additional memory, and while training converges somewhat more slowly than it would with AdamW, the team successfully completes their fine-tuning run within their available hardware, a tradeoff worth making given their specific constraint.
Common Mistakes

items: Dismissing SGD entirely as outdated, when it remains genuinely useful under tight memory constraints
Using plain SGD without momentum and being surprised by slow, zigzagging convergence
Not understanding that Adam and AdamW are direct extensions of the SGD idea rather than an unrelated approach
Assuming SGD always underperforms Adam style optimizers, when the gap depends heavily on the specific task and architecture

blocks.text: Practice

In your own words, explain why using a small random mini-batch to estimate the gradient, rather than the full dataset, makes SGD both faster per step and noisier per step compared to full batch gradient descent.
Key Takeaway

Stochastic gradient descent estimates the true gradient using a small random mini-batch rather than the full dataset, trading some accuracy for far more frequent and memory efficient updates, and it forms the foundational idea that momentum, Adam, and AdamW all build directly on top of, remaining a reasonable choice today specifically when memory constraints are severe.
